table.text: We tested these hypotheses in four pre-registered experiments across 40 countries (total N = 52,508), where participants were randomly assigned to imagine a utopian or dystopian society before making identical likelihood judgments.
U.S. participants were also representative in terms of educational attainment and political ideology.

A binomial general linear mixed model (random intercept and slope by country) showed that participants were far more likely to name at least one leader in the dystopia than the utopia condition, OR = 2.02, 95% CI [1.73, 2.35], z = 9.00, p < .001 (see Figure 2, Panel A).

table.text: Participants' political ideology significantly moderated the difference in Trump mentions between conditions, but not the difference for Putin (see Text S4, Table S8 and Figure S8): The more right-leaning participants were, the smaller the excess of Trump mentions in the dystopia relative to the utopia condition.

After ethics approval from the internal review board at the University of Oslo (Reference number 30444004), data were collected via the panelist provider Prolific between November 28th 2024 and February 28th 2025.
To be eligible, participants had to be aged eighteen years or above, be fluent in English and reside in one of four countries: India, Mexico, South Africa, or the USA.

Participants filled out one item measuring the likelihood of their experimental condition (i.e., utopia/dystopia) to occur (i.e., "How likely do you think it is that such a [utopia/dystopia] will ever happen?"

After approval by the IRB commission of the NHH Norwegian School of Economics (NHH-IRB-2025-91), participants were recruited via the panelist providers Norstat and Dynata between 12th of May and 21st of June 2025 and had to formally consent before taking part in the survey.
Within each country, participants were again randomly assigned to either write about their utopian or dystopian future.
NHH-IRB-2026-155), we conducted Experiment 3 on Qualtrics with recruitment via Prolific on March 30th 2026.
To be eligible, participants had to be aged 18 or above, be American citizens, and provide informed consent.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: 1) dystopia (i.e., write about what it would look like) + leader absence (i.e., not asked about political leaders), 2) utopia + leader absence, 3) dystopia + leader presence (i.e., write about whether a specific political leader may influence the scenario coming true), 4) utopia + leader presence, see Text S8.
Additionally, participants were presented with the same leader attribution and likelihood judgment items as in Experiments 1 and 2.
Participants were recruited via Prolific from March 31st to April 13th 2026.

table.text: A sensitivity analysis in G*Power (Version 3.1, (44)) revealed that in a two-tailed independent samples t-test with an alpha level of .05, the achieved sample for the two groups provided 80% power to detect a Cohen's d effect size of ≥ .20. Based on the same parameters, the 2x4 ANOVA could detect a condition main effect (dfnumerator = 1) of approximately f = .10, corresponding to ηₚ² = .01. For the country main effect and the interaction effect (both dfnumerator = 3), the minimum detectable effect was approximately f = .12, corresponding to ηₚ² = .01. For exploratory moderation analysis, a sensitivity analysis, N = 767, α = .05, indicated our experiment had 80% power to detect interaction effects as small as f² = .01.

table.title: UTO-DYSTO: Causal beliefs about future utopias and dystopias
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
The overarching research question is whether people think societal utopias and dystopias are shaped by different causal forces. Participants will first think and write about either their utopia or their dystopia, and then make a series of judgments about the type of society they have just written about.

As specific hypotheses, we will test the following predictions:
H1a: People will believe it is more likely that their utopia will come true one day than their dystopia.
H1b: People will believe it is more likely that their dystopia will come true one day than their utopia.
H2: People will believe that their own actions have a greater impact on whether their utopia will come true than whether their dystopia will come true.
H3: People will believe that political leaders have a greater impact on whether their dystopia will come true than whether their utopia will come true.
H4: People will believe that it is more a question of random events (good vs. bad luck) whether their dystopia will come true than whether their utopia will come true.
table.design_dependent_variables:
When evaluating either the utopia or dystopia people have in mind, participants will make one judgment of likelihood and three attributional judgments on a response scale from 0-10, using the following items: 
1: How likely do you think it is that such a [utopia/dystopia] will ever happen?
2: To what extent do you think your own actions can affect whether such a [utopia/dystopia] will happen or not?
3: To what extent do you think that political leaders in society can affect whether such a [utopia/dystopia] will happen or not?
4: To what extent do you think it is a question of random events (good vs. bad luck) whether such a [utopia/dystopia] will happen or not?
table.study_design_overview:
Half of the participants will be randomly assigned to one of two experimental conditions, between subjects: Utopian thinking or Dystopian thinking. Please see below for details.

Utopian thinking:
We would like you to imagine a utopian society or world. A utopian society or world is the best imaginable future which you hope or wish for. In the space provided below, please describe what a utopian society or world would be like for you. Also shortly explain what would make this utopian society or world ideal or the best imaginable future. 
There are NO right or wrong answers: We are interested in YOUR IDEAS about what a utopian society would be like. Please try to write a minimum of about 100 words, but spend no more than about 5 minutes on this task.

Dystopian thinking: 
We would like you to imagine a dystopian society or world. A dystopian society or world is the worst imaginable future which you dread or fear. In the space provided below, please describe what a dystopian society or world would be like for you. Also shortly explain what would make this dystopian society or world problematic or the worst imaginable future. 
There are NO right or wrong answers: We are interested in YOUR IDEAS about what a dystopian society would be like. Please try to write a minimum of about 100 words, but spend no more than about 5 minutes on this task.
table.statistical_tests:
For all our hypotheses (H1-H4), we will test each hypothesis using an independent t-test comparing the mean of the relevant outcome variable between our two experimental conditions: Utopian thinking or Dystopian thinking. 

Using an alpha level of 5% (p<.05) in a two-tailed test, a statistically significant difference in the predicted direction will be interpreted as empirical support for the specific hypothesis in question. In addition, we will also report the standardized effect size (Cohen’s d) and the 95% confidence interval for each effect size.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants will be excluded if they fail an attention check at the beginning of the study. When testing each of the four hypotheses, all other participants who complete the full survey will be included in the main analysis.
table.sample_size: Across 4 countries (South Africa, India, Mexico, and the USA), we will collect data from 100 attentive participants per condition, making it 200 participants per country and a total sample of approximately 800 participants.
table.additional_comments: In the primary analysis, the four hypotheses will be tested using the full sample across all four countries. In addition, we will conduct an explorative analysis for each country, to test for possible differences between countries. We will use a two-way ANOVA with a 2 (condition) x 4 (country) design to do so.

table.title: Beliefs about future utopias and dystopias: A global study across 40 countries
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
The overarching research question is whether people think societal utopias and dystopias are shaped by different causal forces and underlying probabilities. 

Participants will first think and write about either their utopia or their dystopia, and then make a series of judgments about the type of society they have just written about. 

We will test the following primary hypotheses:
H1: People will believe it is more likely that their dystopia will come true one day than their utopia.
H2: People will believe that their own actions have a greater impact on whether their utopia will come true than whether their dystopia will come true.
H3: People will believe that political leaders have a greater impact on whether their dystopia will come true than whether their utopia will come true.
table.design_dependent_variables:
This study has three primary outcome measures (DVs). When evaluating either the utopia or dystopia people have in mind, participants will make one judgment of likelihood and two attributional judgments on a response scale from 0-10, using the following items: 

DV1: How likely do you think it is that such a [utopia/dystopia] will ever happen?
(0=Extremely unlikely, 10=Extremely likely)

DV2: To what extent do you think your own actions can affect whether such a [utopia/dystopia] will happen or not?
(0=Not at all, 10=Very much so)

DV3: To what extent do you think that political leaders in society can affect whether such a [utopia/dystopia] will happen or not?
(0=Not at all, 10=Very much so)

After completing the last question about political leaders, participants will then be asked a follow-up question about whether they had any specific leader in mind, and if so, write the name of this leader in an open text box.
table.study_design_overview:
Each participant will be randomly assigned to one of two experimental conditions, between-subjects: Utopian thinking or Dystopian thinking. Please see below for details.

Utopian thinking condition: Instructions
In this part of our study, we would like you to imagine a utopian society or world.

A utopian society or world is the best imaginable future which you hope or wish for. In the space provided below, please describe and explain what a utopian society or world would be like for you, and what would make this utopian society/world the best future you can imagine.

There are NO right or wrong answers: We are interested in YOUR IDEAS about what a utopian society would be like.
Please make sure to stop for a moment, and write one or two sentences to describe your utopia before you proceed.

Dystopian thinking condition: Instructions 
In this part of our study, we would like you to imagine a dystopian society or world.

A dystopian society or world is the worst imaginable future which you dread or fear. In the space provided below, please describe and explain what a dystopian society or world would be like for you, and what would make this dystopian society/world the worst future you can imagine.

There are NO right or wrong answers: We are interested in YOUR IDEAS about what a dystopian society would be like.
Please stop for a moment, and write one or two sentences to describe your dystopia before you proceed.
table.statistical_tests:
Multi-level models will be estimated in R, using the lme4 (or glmmTMB if computation is slow), lmerTest, and emmeans packages. Participants are nested within countries. We will set random intercepts and random slopes as long as models converge. We will use an alpha level of 5% for all tests, in which an effect in the predicted direction at p < .05 (two-tailed) will be interpreted as support for the hypothesis.

For H1: We will test a model with likelihood judgment as the dependent variable and condition as the predictor.
For H2: We will test a model with own action attribution as the dependent variable and condition as the predictor.
For H3: We will test a model with leader attribution as the dependent variable and condition as the predictor.

For each model, in the case of model convergence with random effects and intercepts, we estimate random effects with 95% CIs to obtain information about between-country variation and visualize these.

In addition, we will test whether the predicted main effect of experimental condition (utopia vs. dystopia) on likelihood judgments will be mediated by internal action attribution (H4a) and/or external leader attribution (H4b). Here, we use multilevel SEM to estimate effects, with both mediators added in parallel.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants will be excluded if they fail an attention check at the beginning of the study. When testing each of the hypotheses, all other participants who have completed the respective variable measures will be included in the data analysis.
table.sample_size: This study has a predetermined sample size of 40.000 participants (40 countries; 1000 participants per country). The study is part of a larger data collection, consisting of different but unrelated research projects.
table.additional_comments:
Background variables included in the survey: Age, gender, income, education level, left-right political orientation, self-reported party vote in the last national election.  

Text analysis plan 1: DESCRIPTIONS OF UTOPIA AND DYSTOPIA

In a data-driven, automated manner we will explore the topics that participants mention when describing their utopia or dystopia, whether the topic prevalence differs across and between countries, and by political orientation. The identification of topics will follow an approach similar to this:
1. Detect answer language, store as covariate, apply minimal cleaning; 
2. Generate multilingual sentence embeddings (LaBSE or mpnet-v2); 
3. Extract ~30–60 topics via BERTopic, then refit with Combined CTM to obtain document–topic proportions θ; 
4. Discard or merge low-coherence clusters after human/native-speaker validation; 

We will then present the prevalence of topics across countries and calculate whether certain topics are more prevalent in some countries than others, and for certain political orientations. For every topic we use a logistic multilevel model to fit a regression that treats each participant’s topic share (a number between 0 and 1) as the outcome. We fit the same regression twice—once with the country offsets and once without them—and ask: Does letting countries differ make the model noticeably better? When a topic varies by country, we look at each country’s estimated offset and its 95% confidence range. We repeat this test for all topics and adjust the resulting p-values so that the overall chance of false positives stays acceptably low using Holm correction. Random slopes and intercepts will be added as long as models converge.


Text analysis plan 2: LEADER NAMES

We will code this text response based on whether (1) participants mention a particular leader or not (binary yes/no), (2) which specific leaders are mentioned most often, and (3) the political leaning of the leader mentioned.

(1) is tested using one binomial logistic multilevel model with a binary outcome and condition as predictors. (2) is tested with a multinomial logistic multilevel model (if needed, via the Poisson trick). Random slopes and intercepts will be added as long as models converge. For (3) we test three models. Model 1 tests whether condition predicts the politician’s taxonomic political orientation (vs. no leader, as reference group), using a multinomial logistic multilevel model (if needed, via the Poisson trick). Model 2 tests whether condition predicts the leader’s social political orientation, and Model 3 whether it predicts the leader’s economic political orientation, both with linear regressions as the outcome is continuous. The latter two models are conducted only among participants mentioning a specific leader.

We will also explore with linear multilevel models conducted separately in the two conditions, whether mentioning a given leader name or (b) political leader type (both with “mentioning no leader” as reference group) is associated with the likelihood that a dystopia/utopia is likely to happen. 

We categorize leader names as follows. 
1. Text standardisation – convert to lower-case, possibly strip titles and honorifics (e.g., “President”, “Dr.”), remove punctuation/extra spaces, and transliterate non-Latin scripts to Latin characters (e.g., «蔡英文» → “Tsai Ing-wen”).
2. LLM canonicalisation – send each cleaned string to GPT-4o (temperature = 0) and request three JSON fields:
canonical_name – the standard English form of the leader’s name
wikidata_qid – the corresponding Wikidata identifier if confidence ≥ 0 .80
confidence – 0–1
Routing rules
confidence ≥ 0 .80 → enter automatic clustering
0 .50 – 0 .79 → add to an existing cluster only if (a) the canonical name exactly matches a cluster label or (b) its embedding lies within ε = 0 .12 of a cluster centroid; otherwise flag for manual review
< 0 .50 → always flagged for manual review by two independent coders
3. High-confidence clustering – embed all canonical names with confidence ≥ 0 .80 using the “text-embedding-3-small” model and cluster them with DBSCAN (cosine distance, ε = 0 .12). This merges residual variants such as “Barack H. Obama” and “Barack Obama” without pair-wise comparison of all strings.
4. Cluster inspection & correction – generate a provisional cluster-level table (canonical_name, n_responses, wikidata_qid). Manually inspect the small subset of clusters that contain multiple Q-IDs or include any responses below the 0 .50 confidence threshold, correcting labels or splitting clusters as needed. This step finalises trustworthy cluster_id values.
5. Propagate codes to the participant file – write the validated canonical_name, cluster_id, and (when available) wikidata_qid back to the original participant-level dataset. Every respondent who named a leader now has exactly one leader code, while those who did not (e.g., wrote “my dad”) receive cluster_id = -1. No rows are aggregated or dropped; all subsequent analyses use this participant-level file, and the cluster-level summary from step 4 is kept only for descriptive statistics.

Note that for analyses with leader names, only leaders with at least 50 cases will be included in analyses to ensure robust estimates.

We classify the leader’s political orientation in three ways; the machine classifiers have already been validated against human coders, so no additional checking is required here.

For every leader we prompt GPT-4o (temperature = 0) to return
 ‒ an economic ideology score (1 = strongly progressive, 5 = strongly conservative)
 ‒ a social ideology score (same scale)
 ‒ one category from the adapted Gunther & Diamond typology (eight options: elite-based, religious mass-based, nationalist mass-based, socialist mass-based, ethnicity-based, electoralist, left-libertarian, extreme-right).

For accuracy, we provide pre-tested explanations of each rating in the prompt.

GENERAL NOTE: Due to the somewhat unpredictable performance of these exploratory procedures and models, we will make adjustments to the pipelines in a data-driven and performance-based manner.

table.title: Utopian-dystopian follow-up: How leader presence influences scenario likelihood judgments.
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
The overarching research question is whether people think the likelihood of future societal utopias and dystopias is shaped by the presence of political leaders. Participants will be instructed to write about their imagined utopia OR dystopia, which either will include a political leader OR no instruction to write about a political leader. Afterward, they will be asked to make a judgment about the likelihood of this future society/world ever coming true. We will test two primary hypotheses:
H1: People will believe it is more likely that their dystopia will come true one day than their utopia.
H2: People will believe that their utopia/dystopia is more likely to become true if it includes a specific political leader than if it does not.
table.design_dependent_variables: LIKELIHOOD JUDGMENT: How likely do you think it is that such a (utopia/dystopia) will ever happen? (0= extremely unlikely - 10 = extremely likely). Participants in the utopia condition will only rate the likelihood of their utopia, and participants in the dystopia condition will only rate the likelihood of their dystopia.
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions, in a 2(scenario_condition: utopia vs. dystopia) x 2(leader_condition: leader absence vs. presence) between-subjects design. 


Condition 1: DYSTOPIA + LEADER ABSENCE
In this part of our study, we would like you to imagine a dystopian society or world.
A dystopian society or world is the worst imaginable future which you dread or fear. In the space provided below, please describe and explain what a dystopian society or world would be like for you, and what would make this dystopian society/world the worst future you can imagine.
There are NO right or wrong answers: We are interested in YOUR IDEAS about what a dystopian society or world would be like.
Please stop for a moment, and write two or three sentences to describe your dystopia before you proceed.


Condition 2: UTOPIA + LEADER ABSENCE
In this part of our study, we would like you to imagine a utopian society or world.
A utopian society or world is the best imaginable future which you hope or wish for. In the space provided below, please describe and explain what a utopian society or world would be like for you, and what would make this utopian society/world the best future you can imagine.
There are NO right or wrong answers: We are interested in YOUR IDEAS about what a utopian society or world would be like.
Please make sure to stop for a moment, and write two or three sentences to describe your utopia before you proceed.


Conditions 3 and 4 will use the same general scenario writing first as in Conditions 1 and 2, focusing either on utopia or dystopia. The difference is that Conditions 3 and 4 will contain a follow-up question on a separate screen, asking them to describe how a specific leader could influence their [utopia/dystopia]. Below, we only include this new element of Conditions 3 and 4.
  
Condition 3: DYSTOPIA + LEADER PRESENCE
Based on the dystopian society or world you just wrote about (the worst possible future you can imagine), please consider whether there is a particular political leader you think can affect whether such a dystopia will happen or not.

What is it about this leader and his/her actions that makes you think about this specific person in the context of your dystopia?

Please stop for a moment, and write two or three sentences to name and describe the political leader that you think about right now, before you proceed.


Condition 4: UTOPIA + LEADER PRESENCE
Based on the utopian society or world you just wrote about (the best possible future you can imagine), please consider whether there is a particular political leader you think can affect whether such a utopia will happen or not.

What is it about this leader and his/her actions that makes you think about this specific person in the context of your utopia?

Please stop for a moment, and write two or three sentences to name and describe the political leader that you think about right now, before you proceed.
table.statistical_tests:
We will test our hypotheses using a 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA, first estimating the main effects (model step 1), to test our primary hypotheses predicting main effects (H1 and H2). Afterward, we will also explore whether the hypothesized effect of H2 is moderated by scenario_condition (model step 2). We will use a standard alpha level of 5% in two-tailed tests, in which a mean difference in the predicted direction and a corresponding p-value below 5% will be interpreted as statistically significant support for the specific hypothesis in question (H1 or H2).
To obtain robust estimates that are less sensitive to violations of parametric assumptions, we will compute bootstrapped-based SEs and 95% CIs using 5000 resamples if standard normality and equal variance assumptions are not met.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants will be excluded if they show “low” authenticity in Prolific’s llm or bot checks if verified by a human researcher. Participants will also be excluded if they fail both attention checks.
table.sample_size: A sensitivity analysis was conducted in G*Power 3.1.9.7. For our planned 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA, assuming 90% power, α = .05, and a total sample size of N = 2000 (500 per condition), the minimum detectable effect size for the main and interaction effects was approximately f = .07.
table.additional_comments:
In addition to the primary analysis (H1 and H2), we will also explore the following: 
1) whether the relationship specified in H2 is moderated by the scenario_condition. Specifically, we will explore whether the effect proposed in H2 differs across the dystopia and utopia conditions. 
2) whether there are main effects of scenario_condition on whether the leader is perceived as a) competent, b) warm, and c) moral. Note that we will only explore this question for participants assigned to conditions 3 or 4, based on a follow-up scale response rating of the perceived traits of the specific leader they thought about and wrote about as part of the leader presence manipulation. In addition, we will explore these leader perceptions as potential mediating variables of the predicted main effects on scenario likelihood.
3) We also included the following leader attribution item as a secondary measure: “To what extent do you think that political leaders in society can affect whether such a (utopia/dystopia)  will happen or not?” (0 = not at all - 10 = very much so). We will explore potential condition effects, i.e., whether leadership attribution is indeed higher in the leader presence (vs. absence) condition.

We also include 
a)  the following demographic variables: age, education, gender, ethnicity, political orientation, political affiliation, area of residence, income
b)  Comprehension check: To what extent do you agree with each statement below? (not at all, to some extent, very much)
- At this moment, I have an idea of what the (worst/best) imaginable society might look like.
- Right now, I think about what sort of world I would (dislike/like) most to live in. 
c) the following exploratory variables: leader morality, warmth, and competence.

Leader characteristics:
Perceived morality, warmth, and competence will be measured with 3 items each, using the following instruction.
When answering our previous question asking if you could write about a specific political leader that you thought about in the context of your dystopia, how would you describe the personal traits and characteristics of this leader?

Please use the scale below to indicate to what extent you agree or disagree that each word is a good description of your general impression of what this leader is like as a person.

If you did not think about any particular leader when responding to that writing question, please leave these questions unanswered and proceed.

I would consider the specific political leader I wrote about to be:
Likable
Friendly
Warm
Intelligent
Competent
Skilled
Honest
Fair
Trustworthy

Text analysis plan 1: DESCRIPTIONS OF UTOPIA AND DYSTOPIA

In a data-driven, automated manner we will explore the topics that participants mention when describing their utopia or dystopia, whether the topic prevalence differs across and between countries, and by political orientation. The identification of topics will follow an approach similar to this:
1. Detect answer language, store as covariate, apply minimal cleaning;
2. Generate multilingual sentence embeddings (LaBSE or mpnet-v2);
3. Extract ~30–60 topics via BERTopic, then refit with Combined CTM to obtain document–topic proportions θ;
4. Discard or merge low-coherence clusters after human/native-speaker validation;

We will then present the prevalence of topics across countries and calculate whether certain topics are more prevalent in some countries than others, and for certain political orientations. For every topic we use a logistic multilevel model to fit a regression that treats each participant’s topic share (a number between 0 and 1) as the outcome. We fit the same regression twice—once with the country offsets and once without them—and ask: Does letting countries differ make the model noticeably better? When a topic varies by country, we look at each country’s estimated offset and its 95% confidence range. We repeat this test for all topics and adjust the resulting p-values so that the overall chance of false positives stays acceptably low using Holm correction. Random slopes and intercepts will be added as long as models converge.


Text analysis plan 2: LEADER NAMES

We will code this text response based on whether (1) participants mention a particular leader or not (binary yes/no), (2) which specific leaders are mentioned most often, and (3) the political leaning of the leader mentioned.

(1) is tested using one binomial logistic multilevel model with a binary outcome and condition as predictors. (2) is tested with a multinomial logistic multilevel model (if needed, via the Poisson trick). Random slopes and intercepts will be added as long as models converge. For (3) we test three models. Model 1 tests whether condition predicts the politician’s taxonomic political orientation (vs. no leader, as reference group), using a multinomial logistic multilevel model (if needed, via the Poisson trick). Model 2 tests whether condition predicts the leader’s social political orientation, and Model 3 whether it predicts the leader’s economic political orientation, both with linear regressions as the outcome is continuous. The latter two models are conducted only among participants mentioning a specific leader.

We will also explore with linear multilevel models conducted separately in the two conditions, whether mentioning a given leader name or (b) political leader type (both with “mentioning no leader” as reference group) is associated with the likelihood that a dystopia/utopia is likely to happen.

We categorize leader names as follows.
1. Text standardisation – convert to lower-case, possibly strip titles and honorifics (e.g., “President”, “Dr.”), remove punctuation/extra spaces, and transliterate non-Latin scripts to Latin characters (e.g., «蔡英文» → “Tsai Ing-wen”).
2. LLM canonicalisation – send each cleaned string to GPT-4o (temperature = 0) and request three JSON fields:
canonical_name – the standard English form of the leader’s name
wikidata_qid – the corresponding Wikidata identifier if confidence ≥ 0 .80
confidence – 0–1
Routing rules
confidence ≥ 0 .80 → enter automatic clustering
0 .50 – 0 .79 → add to an existing cluster only if (a) the canonical name exactly matches a cluster label or (b) its embedding lies within ε = 0 .12 of a cluster centroid; otherwise flag for manual review
< 0 .50 → always flagged for manual review by two independent coders
3. High-confidence clustering – embed all canonical names with confidence ≥ 0 .80 using the “text-embedding-3-small” model and cluster them with DBSCAN (cosine distance, ε = 0 .12). This merges residual variants such as “Barack H. Obama” and “Barack Obama” without pair-wise comparison of all strings.
4. Cluster inspection & correction – generate a provisional cluster-level table (canonical_name, n_responses, wikidata_qid). Manually inspect the small subset of clusters that contain multiple Q-IDs or include any responses below the 0 .50 confidence threshold, correcting labels or splitting clusters as needed. This step finalises trustworthy cluster_id values.
5. Propagate codes to the participant file – write the validated canonical_name, cluster_id, and (when available) wikidata_qid back to the original participant-level dataset. Every respondent who named a leader now has exactly one leader code, while those who did not (e.g., wrote “my dad”) receive cluster_id = -1. No rows are aggregated or dropped; all subsequent analyses use this participant-level file, and the cluster-level summary from step 4 is kept only for descriptive statistics.

Note that for analyses with leader names, only leaders with at least 50 cases will be included in analyses to ensure robust estimates.

We classify the leader’s political orientation in three ways; the machine classifiers have already been validated against human coders, so no additional checking is required here.

For every leader we prompt GPT-4o (temperature = 0) to return
‒ an economic ideology score (1 = strongly progressive, 5 = strongly conservative)
‒ a social ideology score (same scale)
‒ one category from the adapted Gunther & Diamond typology (eight options: elite-based, religious mass-based, nationalist mass-based, socialist mass-based, ethnicity-based, electoralist, left-libertarian, extreme-right).

For accuracy, we provide pre-tested explanations of each rating in the prompt.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .09", "ps < .01", "ps > .05", 
"ps > .05"), Text = c("However, we observed no significant mediational effects of scenario likelihood via attribution to self or chance (ps > .09, Text S2, Figure S3), meaning that leader attribution was the only significant mediator.", 
"Furthermore, there was a significant difference in likelihood judgment between all countries (all ps < .01), except for South Africa and Mexico (p = .999).", 
"Constraining any of the other paths did not significantly worsen model fit (all ps > .05), suggesting no significant difference between the countries for these paths.", 
"The total indirect effect of condition on likelihood was significant in the USA (β = .04, b = .20, 95% CI [.01, .39], SE = .10, z = 2.03, p = .042), but not in India, Mexico, or South Africa (all ps > .05)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. live_data_statements: We tested these hypotheses in four pre-registered experiments across 40 countries (total N = 52,508), where participants were randomly assigned to imagine a utopian or dystopian society before making identical likelihood judgments.
U.S. participants were also representative in terms of educational attainment and political ideology.

A binomial general linear mixed model (random intercept and slope by country) showed that participants were far more likely to name at least one leader in the dystopia than the utopia condition, OR = 2.02, 95% CI [1.73, 2.35], z = 9.00, p < .001 (see Figure 2, Panel A).

Participants' political ideology significantly moderated the difference in Trump mentions between conditions, but not the difference for Putin (see Text S4, Table S8 and Figure S8): The more right-leaning participants were, the smaller the excess of Trump mentions in the dystopia relative to the utopia condition.
Participants were representative in terms of sex for all countries and ethnicity for all except India.
US participants were also populationrepresentative in terms of educational attainment and political ideology.

After ethics approval from the internal review board at the University of Oslo (Reference number 30444004), data were collected via the panelist provider Prolific between November 28th 2024 and February 28th 2025.
To be eligible, participants had to be aged eighteen years or above, be fluent in English and reside in one of four countries: India, Mexico, South Africa, or the USA.

Participants filled out one item measuring the likelihood of their experimental condition (i.e., utopia/dystopia) to occur (i.e., "How likely do you think it is that such a [utopia/dystopia] will ever happen?"

After approval by the IRB commission of the NHH Norwegian School of Economics (NHH-IRB-2025-91), participants were recruited via the panelist providers Norstat and Dynata between 12th of May and 21st of June 2025 and had to formally consent before taking part in the survey.
Within each country, participants were again randomly assigned to either write about their utopian or dystopian future.
NHH-IRB-2026-155), we conducted Experiment 3 on Qualtrics with recruitment via Prolific on March 30th 2026.
To be eligible, participants had to be aged 18 or above, be American citizens, and provide informed consent.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: 1) dystopia (i.e., write about what it would look like) + leader absence (i.e., not asked about political leaders), 2) utopia + leader absence, 3) dystopia + leader presence (i.e., write about whether a specific political leader may influence the scenario coming true), 4) utopia + leader presence, see Text S8.
Additionally, participants were presented with the same leader attribution and likelihood judgment items as in Experiments 1 and 2.
Participants were recruited via Prolific from March 31st to April 13th 2026.
None of the participants failed both attention checks, accordingly no participants were excluded based on attention-check performance.
Participants were randomly assigned to a 2x2 design.
Participants were presented with the same leader attribution and likelihood judgment items as in Experiments 1, 2, and 3.

Specifically, the more conservative participants were, they less likely they were to mention electoralist and social mass-based leaders in the utopia condition and somewhat more likely to mention them in the dystopia condition.

By contrast, the more conservative participants were, the more likely they were to mention extreme-right and nationalist mass-based leaders in the utopia condition and the less likely they were to mention nationalist mass-based leaders in the dystopia condition.
As visualized in Figure S14, left-leaning participants were most likely to mention right-leaning leaders in the dystopia condition and left-leaning leaders in the utopia condition.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions, in a 2(scenario condition: utopia vs. dystopia) x 2(leader condition: low vs. high leader impact) betweensubjects design.
Participants were grouped by country (i.e., India, Mexico, South Africa, USA).

To test whether particular leaders were more (or less) likely to be named when participants had thought of a dystopia versus a utopia, we first isolated the 14 names that formed the union of each condition's ten most-frequent answers.

info.title: Global Collective Pessimism: People predict a dystopian future and attribute it to political leaders

author.affiliation:
Department of Strategy and Management
								Norwegian School of Economics

Department of Psychology 3 BI Norwegian Business School
								Department of Communication and Culture
								University of Oslo

text.text: Personal optimism is widespread.
This research provides cross-cultural evidence for collective pessimism.
Across four pre-registered experiments in 40 countries (N = 52,508), people believed it is much more likely that a future dystopian society will materialize than a utopian society.

Dystopian predictions were driven not by internal attribution, but by asymmetric external attribution: People believed political leaders in society can exert greater influence on dystopian than utopian world development, and high leader impact was correlationally and causally linked to higher scenario likelihood.
Text-based analyses revealed that participants named a political leader nearly twice as often in dystopias than utopias, and such personalized dystopias were considered more likely.
Dystopian predictions were stronger among left-leaning individuals and in rich democracies, yet generalized across ideologies and world regions.
Humans are prospective creatures (1) (2) (3), and individuals across the world tend to be remarkably optimistic about their own future.
text.formatted: Humans are prospective creatures <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>, and individuals across the world tend to be remarkably optimistic about their own future.

text.text: In one 16-country survey, 89% of the participants expected their personal lives to improve over the next five years (4).
Yet, when asked about society as a whole in a different survey, only 35% expected global living conditions to improve (5).
text.formatted: Yet, when asked about society as a whole in a different survey, only 35% expected global living conditions to improve <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: This asymmetry matters because future-oriented thinking, or prospection, shapes well-being (6, 7), cooperation (8, 9), moral decision-making (10, 11), collective action (12, 13), and politics (14, 15), and because political movements increasingly mobilize voters around narratives of societal decline (16).
text.formatted: This asymmetry matters because future-oriented thinking, or prospection, shapes well-being (6, 7), cooperation (8, 9), moral decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11)</ref>, collective action <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13)</ref>, and politics <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15)</ref>, and because political movements increasingly mobilize voters around narratives of societal decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Research in psychology and behavioral science has focused almost exclusively on individual prospection.
Here we study collective prospection (17, 18), focusing on how people judge the likelihood that a future utopian or dystopian society will one day come true, and what drives those predictions.
text.formatted: Here we study collective prospection <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18)</ref>, focusing on how people judge the likelihood that a future utopian or dystopian society will one day come true, and what drives those predictions.

text.text: We test whether people across 40 countries covering all world regions consider a dystopian future more likely than a utopian one, and whether this asymmetry reflects how people attribute societal outcomes to political leaders.
Research on individual prospection typically finds personal optimism.
For instance, people commit the 'planning fallacy' by underestimating the required time and resources needed to complete future tasks (19, 20).
text.formatted: For instance, people commit the 'planning fallacy' by underestimating the required time and resources needed to complete future tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20)</ref>.

text.text: They also overestimate the probability of positive life events and underestimate their own risk of negative events (21) (22) (23).
text.formatted: They also overestimate the probability of positive life events and underestimate their own risk of negative events <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref>.

text.text: Optimism persists even under explicit instructions to be realistic, because best-case scenarios come first to mind and crowd out worst-case alternatives (24).
text.formatted: Optimism persists even under explicit instructions to be realistic, because best-case scenarios come first to mind and crowd out worst-case alternatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>.

text.text: Personal optimism is driven by a combination of cognitive and motivational processes (for reviews, see (25, 26)), and critically, is often rooted in internal attribution: People are more optimistic about future events they believe to be largely under their own control (27, 28).
text.formatted: Personal optimism is driven by a combination of cognitive and motivational processes (for reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26)</ref>), and critically, is often rooted in internal attribution: People are more optimistic about future events they believe to be largely under their own control <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28)</ref>.

text.text: There are exceptions from personal optimism (29), whereas the most relevant one for the current research is that people tend to shift towards pessimism for important events considered to be beyond their control (30).
text.formatted: There are exceptions from personal optimism <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref>, whereas the most relevant one for the current research is that people tend to shift towards pessimism for important events considered to be beyond their control <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref>.

text.text: Far less is known about the balance between optimism and pessimism when people consider the collective future of society as a whole.
To our knowledge, no large-scale crosscultural experiments have examined the perceived likelihood of utopian versus dystopian societies.
The few existing studies point toward society-level pessimism rather than optimism.
People are roughly twice as likely to predict economic decline for their country as for themselves (31).

text.text: Whereas positive events come to mind first and are judged more likely in individual prospection (24, 32, 33), one study found the reverse fluency pattern for collective prospection (34), in which participants generated negative future societal events more readily than positive ones.
text.formatted: Whereas positive events come to mind first and are judged more likely in individual prospection <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33)</ref>, one study found the reverse fluency pattern for collective prospection <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(34)</ref>, in which participants generated negative future societal events more readily than positive ones.

text.text: Importantly, that work assessed the fluency of event generation, not optimism versus pessimism in the form of likelihood judgments, and it was conducted in a narrow cultural context (the United States and Canada).
Whether people globally believe a dystopian future is more likely than a utopian one, and why, currently remains unknown.
Our primary hypothesis (H1), predicting collective pessimism, is that people across the world will judge a dystopian society as more likely to come true than a utopian society.

Second, we propose that this type of pessimism is rooted in how societal outcomes are attributed, as people might believe that political leaders are capable of exerting greater influence on dystopian than utopian world development (H2).
As our theoretical framework for these pre-registered hypotheses, we combine two mechanisms: The negativity bias in human psychology and asymmetric leader attribution.

First, the negativity bias refers to a general principle in which "bad is stronger than good" ( (35); see also (36)), meaning that negative information, life events, and experiences have greater impact than the positive equivalent on a range of outcomes, including attention, emotion, first impressions, learning, memory, romantic relationships, and moral judgment.
text.formatted: First, the negativity bias refers to a general principle in which "bad is stronger than good" ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35)</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(36)</ref>), meaning that negative information, life events, and experiences have greater impact than the positive equivalent on a range of outcomes, including attention, emotion, first impressions, learning, memory, romantic relationships, and moral judgment.

text.text: It is currently unclear, however, if and when the negativity bias applies to prospective thinking.

Whereas research on individual prospection tends to find personal optimism, reflecting a positivity bias, we suggest that in collective prospection, the negative dimension will dominate the likelihood judgment.
Second, we propose that attributional inference, meaning how ordinary people explain the internal versus external causation of events (37), plays a key role in this type of future thinking (27, 28).
text.formatted: Second, we propose that attributional inference, meaning how ordinary people explain the internal versus external causation of events <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(37)</ref>, plays a key role in this type of future thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, when the future in question is society's rather than one's own, the outcome should feel less tied to one's own intentions and actions, thereby removing the self-attributional basis for optimism.
An external force we consider especially important in this context is the top-down impact of political leaders.

The "side-effect effect" documented by experimental philosophers shows that people are more willing to attribute harmful than helpful outcomes to the intentional agency of leaders (38), suggesting an asymmetry in how outcomes are linked to powerful agents.
text.formatted: The "side-effect effect" documented by experimental philosophers shows that people are more willing to attribute harmful than helpful outcomes to the intentional agency of leaders <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(38)</ref>, suggesting an asymmetry in how outcomes are linked to powerful agents.

text.text: In that paradigm, participants read about a situation where the outcome was known and had already occurred, and then judged whether the agent brought it about intentionally.
We propose a prospective extension of this mechanism, operating forward in time on society-level beliefs, where the prediction of future worlds will follow a similar leader-driven asymmetry.

We tested these hypotheses in four pre-registered experiments across 40 countries (total N = 52,508), where participants were randomly assigned to imagine a utopian or dystopian society before making identical likelihood judgments.
In Experiments 1, 2, and 3, people evaluated the likelihood of future scenarios generated and written by themselves.
In Experiment 4, people evaluated fixed and content-symmetric scenarios written by the research team based on common themes identified in the participant-generated scenarios in Experiments 1 and 2.
The leader-attribution mechanism was tested using both observed mediation (Experiments 1 and 2) and experimental manipulation of the mediator in a causal-chain design (Experiments 3 and 4).

Beyond the primary hypotheses, we examined whether self-generated dystopias are more often personalized around specific political leaders than utopias and whether such personalized dystopias are judged more likely; explored variation in dystopian predictions across individual-level political ideology and country-level wealth and democracy; and identified the most common themes in self-generated utopias and dystopias.

text.text: Experiments 3 and 4.
Our observational mediation results from Experiments 1 and 2 suggest that the likelihood judgment of a future societal scenario is partly a function of political leader attribution.

To isolate the leader attribution mechanism, we moved beyond the correlational approach and conducted two final studies experimentally manipulating the mediator in a 2 × 2 design, in Experiments 3 and 4.
This design permits testing our proposed explanation as a causal-chain model (Dystopia vs.
Utopia → Leader attribution → Scenario Likelihood), and is considered a superior approach to mechanism evidence in psychology (e.g., (39)).
text.formatted: Utopia → Leader attribution → Scenario Likelihood), and is considered a superior approach to mechanism evidence in psychology (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(39)</ref>).

text.text: Observed mediation infers the mediator-to-outcome path from association alone, under strong assumptions about causal direction and no confounding.
Experiments 3 and 4 provide the missing experimental test of that path.
We predicted that random assignment to high (vs. low) perceived impact of political leaders would lead to higher subsequent likelihood judgments for their given scenario coming true.

Whereas Experiment 3 relied on self-generated scenarios, a final extension is that Experiment 4 introduced fixed and topic-symmetric scenarios between conditions, to rule out the possibility that the main effect and mediation findings in Experiments 1 and 2 were due to participants thinking about utopias and dystopias in different domains.
Both final experiments were conducted in general population online samples from the United States, which were representative with respect to age, gender, and ethnicity.

In Experiment 3 (N = 2,029, see Table S17 for details), participants generated their own utopian or dystopian scenarios as before, but were then asked to think about a specific political leader while doing so or given no such leader instruction, in a 2 (scenario: utopia vs. dystopia) × 2 (leader salience: present vs. absent) between-subjects design.

text.text: Again, there was no evidence for an interaction effect, see Text S10.

These findings in Experiment 4 replicate the central results from Experiment 3 using standardized and topic-symmetric scenarios describing a future dystopia or utopia, identifying robust causal main effects for both scenario and leader impact conditions on likelihood.

The absence of an interaction in both experiments is consistent with the proposed causal chain, in which scenario type (dystopia vs. utopia) shapes how much impact people attribute to political leaders (Experiments 1 and 2), and high attributed leader impact in turn raises the perceived likelihood of whichever scenario is under consideration (Experiments 3 and 4), rather than leader impact operating on dystopian scenarios alone.
The nature of dystopian and utopian worlds has been richly portrayed in classic literature, film, and modern TV series, suggesting they play a prominent role in human imagination.
How most people actually think about such alternative societies has received less attention in psychology and the behavioral sciences.
In the current research, we provide global evidence of the content, drivers, and perceived likelihood of dystopian versus utopian societies.

Whereas research on individual prediction tends to find personal optimism, the current research reveals pervasive collective pessimism: Data from four pre-registered experiments in 40 countries (N = 52,508), found that people assessed a future dystopian society as significantly more likely than a utopian one.
This tendency was substantial, and persisted across both self-generated and fixed scenarios, appearing in 35 of the 40 countries.
Furthermore, self-generated dystopias were about twice as likely as utopias to be personalized around a specific political leader.

In terms of the mechanism, we found both observed mediation and experimental causal-chain evidence supporting our proposed explanation of asymmetric leader attribution: People believe that political leaders in society can have a greater impact on dystopian than utopian world development, and this belief is one important driver of the dystopian dominance in collective prediction.
The theoretical implications of this research emerge along three distinct lines.
First, they delineate a boundary condition for the extensively documented optimism in individual prospective thinking.
Specifically, when the anticipated future pertains to society at large rather than personal circumstances, a negativity bias appears to supersede such optimism.
This observation expands the psychological axiom that "bad is stronger than good" (35) into the domain of collective future cognition.
Second, the research extends attribution theory (37).
text.formatted: Second, the research extends attribution theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(37)</ref>.

text.text: The asymmetry that links harmful "side-effect" outcomes more to powerful agents than helpful outcomes (38) has been studied for outcomes that have already occurred.
text.formatted: The asymmetry that links harmful "side-effect" outcomes more to powerful agents than helpful outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(38)</ref> has been studied for outcomes that have already occurred.

text.text: We show that it also shapes predictions about future societies that do not yet exist.

Third and finally, the results invite the possibility that personal optimism and collective pessimism are mirror images of an identical attributional logic: While individuals may perceive themselves as largely controlling their own futures, we find that they view the collective future as dependent on powerful external actors who are presumed to cause more harm than good.
We must consider alternative interpretations.
The prevalence of dystopian narratives may stem from a structural asymmetry rather than inherent pessimism.
Whereas a utopia may demand simultaneous perfection across all variables, a dystopia may for some people require only partial failure.
Experiment 4 speaks against this hypothesis, as participants rated the dystopian scenario more than twice as probable even when content domains were controlled and only valence differed.
Disproportionate exposure to negative news may well contribute to the baseline asymmetry in likelihood judgment, but it cannot explain the attributional pattern we also observed.
In our view, a media-exposure account does not predict that randomly assigning people to perceive high leader influence would raise likelihood judgments.
It also does not predict that this manipulation would work equally for utopian and dystopian scenarios, as it did in Experiments 3 and 4.
Several limitations persist.

Although our samples covered all global regions, they relied on online panels rather than fully representative populations and underrepresented African countries; the causal tests of the leader-to-likelihood pathway (Experiments 3 and 4) were restricted to the United States; and our methodology assessed beliefs about extreme hypothetical futures rather than calibrated forecasts.
Notably, the dystopian prediction effect was absent or reversed in a small, yet populous subset of nations in Experiment 2, including India and China.
For India, this contrasts with Experiment 1, where the effect was significant in a smaller sample.

Because that Indian sample was less representative in age, gender, and ethnicity than the sample in Experiment 2, we regard the larger and more representative Experiment 2 estimate as the better guide, and treat the Indian result as unsettled.

Generally, the observed variation does not undermine the generalizability, but aligns with our moderation findings: Collective pessimism was found in most countries, but it peaked in wealthy and established democracies, and waned or even reversed in contexts where recent lived trajectories rose sharply, suggesting that dystopian predictions are not merely an extension of adverse present conditions.
The cross-cultural findings issue a cautionary note for liberal democracies.
It was within affluent, democratic nations that collective pessimism proved most acute.

Consequently, political campaigns leveraging stories of societal decay may encounter considerable support in these contexts (16), particularly amid a decade of documented global democratic decline (42, 43).
text.formatted: Consequently, political campaigns leveraging stories of societal decay may encounter considerable support in these contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>, particularly amid a decade of documented global democratic decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43)</ref>.

text.text: When the public perceives dystopian outcomes as more probable than utopian ones and attributes asymmetric power to actualize them to political leaders, believable optimism regarding our collective future becomes a rare commodity.
Thus, presenting plausible and positive societal visions may hold equal significance for sustaining democracy as highlighting the dangers of democratic decline.
At a broader level, this paper shifts the analytical focus of prospection research from the individual person in a single cultural context to collective cognition, at societal scale across the world.

The results indicate that a global majority express collective pessimism by predicting that a dystopian future is more likely than a utopian future, and consider the asymmetric impact of political leaders to be one important part of the explanation.

Sample size was determined apriori based on financial constraints.
Participants were representative in terms of sex for all countries and ethnicity for all except India.
US participants were also populationrepresentative in terms of educational attainment and political ideology.

text.text: After ethics approval from the internal review board at the University of Oslo (Reference number 30444004), data were collected via the panelist provider Prolific between November 28th 2024 and February 28th 2025.
To be eligible, participants had to be aged eighteen years or above, be fluent in English and reside in one of four countries: India, Mexico, South Africa, or the USA.
The experiment took place on Qualtrics.
Each one half of the participants per country were randomly assigned to the utopia and the other half to the dystopia condition.
Those assigned to the utopia condition were instructed to imagine their best imaginable future society or world.
They were then cued to write a minimum of about 100 words about what their vision entailed and what made it utopian.
Those in the dystopia condition received the equivalent instructions but focused on their worst imaginable future society or world (see Text S6 for instructions).
Manipulation Check.

After having described their utopia or dystopia, participants' state utopian thinking (e.g., "At the moment, I have an idea of what the ideal society might look like."; r(765) = .59, p < .001) and state dystopian thinking (e.g., "At the moment, I have an idea of what the worst imaginable society might look like."; r(765) = .60, p < .001) were assessed with two items each that were measured on Likert scales ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

text.text: Probability Judgement.

Participants filled out one item measuring the likelihood of their experimental condition (i.e., utopia/dystopia) to occur (i.e., "How likely do you think it is that such a [utopia/dystopia] will ever happen?"
; 0 extremely unlikely to 10 extremely likely).
Attribution Measures.

Participants also completed three single-item attribution measures regarding the realization of their utopia/dystopia: 1) attributed internal control (i.e., "To what extent do you think your own actions can affect whether such a [utopia/dystopia] will happen or not?"), 2) attributed political leaders' control (i.e., "To what extent do you think that political leaders in society can affect whether such a [utopia/dystopia] will happen or not?"), and 3) attributed role of luck (i.e., "To what extent do you think it is a question of luck vs. unluck (random events) whether such a [utopia/dystopia] will happen or not?").
Responses were scored on Likert scales ranging from 0 (not at all) to 10 (very much).
Demographics.
We assessed age, gender, marital status, citizenship, religious affiliation, migration background, education, and employment status.

Furthermore, political orientation was measured in three distinct ways: 1) on an 11-point scale, progressing from 0 (far left) to 5 (center) to 10 (far right), 2) on a slider asking participants to indicate their political orientation regarding social issues, e.g., race relations, gender roles, from0 = liberal to100 = conservative, and 3) on a slider asking participants to indicate their political orientation regarding economic issues, e.g., taxes, public spending, again ranging from0 = liberal to100 = conservative.
The analyses were conducted in two phases.
In Step 1, we tested our pre-registered hypotheses via t-tests, Welch's tests where homogeneity assumptions were violated, and 2 (utopia vs. dystopia) x 4 (country) Analyses of Variance (ANOVA).
In Step 2, we ran exploratory analyses to tease out additional, non-pre-registered patterns.
To do so, we assessed moderation of the hypothesized effects by political orientation.

Additionally, we conducted multi-group parallel-mediation analyses to examine whether the experimental effect on likelihood was mediated by our three attribution measures (i.e., internal control, political leaders' control, and luck).
Participants who did not follow the task were manually excluded via Excel.
All other analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.2, ( 45)) via the R Studio interface.

text.text: Before any machine learning, every free-text answer passed through a language-agnostic cleaning pipeline.

Honorifics such as "Prime Minister" or "Pres." were stripped with a regular expression; excess white-space and punctuation were normalized; for Latin-script strings only, letters were transliterated to ASCII with unidecode, while Chinese, Cyrillic and other non-Latin scripts were left intact.
A second expression split multi-name strings on commas, slashes or the word "and" in fifteen languages.
The langdetect package v.
1.0.9 (61)) then attempted to identify the interface language, returning "unknown" for very short strings.
Literal placeholders such as "none", "不知道" or "없음" were mapped to an id_status code of no_input, and a set of survey-instruction fragments in East-Asian languages was deleted.

After this stage the data comprised 18,189 candidate strings: 62.8 percent were ultimately identified as valid leader names, 33.3 percent remained unidentified, and 3.9 percent contained no processable input.
Canonicalization relied on the GPT-4o-mini model served through the OpenAI v1.68.2 API.
For every unique cleaned string an asynchronous call requested a single JSON object containing an English name, a Wikidata Q-ID, and a confidence score from zero to one.
The prompt included the respondent's ISO country code and detected interface language so that, for example, "总统习近平" from a Chinese respondent resolved to "Xi Jinping."
We accepted returned names whose confidence was at least 0.80.
Any lowerconfidence variant was fitted against the high-confidence list with RapidFuzz; a similarity of ninety or above replaced the variant with its already accepted counterpart.

To merge near-duplicates that nonetheless survived canonicalization, the accepted names were embedded with sentence-transformers (all-mpnet-base-v2) and clustered using DBSCAN with a cosine-distance threshold of 0.12.
Each cluster received an integer ID, and singletons took an ID above one hundred thousand.
The cluster lookup was merged back into the full long file.

As pre-registered, we first modelled whether each respondent named at least one leader using a binomial mixed-effects model with condition as the fixed effect and random intercepts and slopes by country.

Second, for the union of the ten most frequent names per condition, we estimated separate leader-specific mixed models (or ordinary logistic models when only one country supplied names) to assess whether a given leader was more likely in the dystopia or utopia narrative.
Third, additional linear mixed models within each condition then asked whether mentioning a leader predicted judged likelihood of the future scenario.

We also conducted various additional tests, examining the role of a leader's ideological profile, see Text S5, Figures S11-14, Tables S9-11, and testing the effect of mentioning specific leaders on leader attribution and likelihood judgments, see Text S3.

To achieve our initial pre-registered target pool of 30-60 topics, whilst ensuring balance between local and global topics and wide representation yet limited noise, we set the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) tuning parameters to neighboring sample points = 17 for utopia and 20 for dystopia, whilst keeping the dimensionality components at 5 and minimum distance at .1 consistent across the conditions.

The Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with noise (HDBSCAN) parameters were set to a minimum cluster size of 74 for utopia and 65 for dystopia, while keeping minimum samples consistent across the two conditions at 10.
Note that the cluster selection method was set to "leaf" to ensure nuanced clusters.

Note that whereas we had pre-registered refitting the topics identified by BERTopic with a combined contextualized topic model (CTM) to obtain document-topic proportions, we deviated from this plan, using BERTopic's built-in "calculate_probabilities()" function instead to directly generate topic-assignment probabilities from our final BERTopic models.

We did so to retain a single modeling framework rather than combining two different topic models, and because this function allowed us to receive the document-level topic information needed for our planned descriptive country and political orientation comparisons.
As a result, all topicprevalence findings reflect BERTopic-derived probabilities, not combined CTM-derived proportions.
Next, as pre-registered, we assessed whether topic prevalence differed across countries.
To do so, we estimated multilevel ordered beta regressions using glmmTMB (75, 76), comparing models with and without country-level random intercepts.

Furthermore, to test whether topic prevalences differed across political orientation, we included political orientation as a fixed effect, representing its average association across countries, and included country-specific random slopes for political orientation, allowing the association to vary across countries.
Holm (77) corrections were applied per condition to control the family-wise error rate.
We also explored whether our macro-level indicators moderated the effects of our experimental conditions on likelihood judgment and leader attribution.
For each dependent variable, we ran a separate model for each macro-level indicator, entering one macro level indicator at a time.
All moderators were standardized prior to analysis.
Models were fitted with the bobyqa optimizer in lme4 (46) to improve convergence.
For all models except for GDP, where it served as predictor and HDI, where it is part of the index, we also controlled for GDP to adjust for macroeconomic differences between countries.

To account for violations of normality and homogeneity, we re-estimated the models using wild bootstrapping with Rademacher weights and HC2 heteroscadisticityconsistent covariance estimator based on 5,000 bootstrap replications via the lmeresampler (55) package.
Holm (77) correction was applied to limit the familywise type I error rate across the moderation tests.
To show regions of significance, we estimated Johnson-Neyman plots via the interactions (48) package.
Finally, we modeled separate linear mixed-effects models per condition for each condition's topic probability with random intercepts for each country.

Note that because all topic probabilities sum to 1 when including the outlier topic, and thus, a higher probability assigned to one topic necessarily reduces the probability assigned to the other topics, coefficients should be interpreted as relative associations.
The same wild bootstrapping procedure as for the moderation models was applied, followed by Holm (77) correction to account for multiple comparisons.

text.text: Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: 1) dystopia (i.e., write about what it would look like) + leader absence (i.e., not asked about political leaders), 2) utopia + leader absence, 3) dystopia + leader presence (i.e., write about whether a specific political leader may influence the scenario coming true), 4) utopia + leader presence, see Text S8.
Additionally, participants were presented with the same leader attribution and likelihood judgment items as in Experiments 1 and 2.
