text.text: Three groups of leaders emerge.
First, several leaders are disproportionately evoked when participants imagine dystopia.
Kim Jong-un, Adolf Hitler, Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump, Viktor Orbán, Gustavo Petro, and Xi Jinping are named more often when thinking about dystopia.
Second, a middle cluster, mentioning Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Cyril Ramaphosa, Prabowo Subianto, and Javier Milei, shows no significant difference between conditions.
Third, Barack Obama, Imran Khan and Narendra Modi are more likely to be cited in the utopian condition.
The specific leaders mentioned in each country can be explored using our Shiny App (https://dystopia-utopia.shinyapps.io/country/).
text.formatted: The specific leaders mentioned in each country can be explored using our Shiny App (<ref type="url" target="https://dystopia-utopia.shinyapps.io/country/">https://dystopia- utopia.shinyapps.io/country/</ref>).

text.text: Notably, Donald Trump was the most frequently named leader in 12 countries and the second-most in 10 countries under the utopia condition, and this rose to 19 countries as first choice and 16 as runner-up under dystopia.
Vladimir Putin was the next most common: in the utopia condition he topped the list in 2 countries and came second in 3, while under dystopia he was first in 5 countries and second in 8.
As pre-registered, we also tested whether participants mentioning specific leaders (vs. no leader) would be associated with the likelihood of the utopia or dystopia happening.
For every leader-frame pair we fitted mixed-effects models predicting the likelihood judgment score from a dummy indicating whether that leader was named (reference = named no one).

As displayed in Figure S9 (also see Table S9 for test statistics), for utopia, mentioning Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Prabowo Subianto, Narendra Modi, or Javier Milei was statistically significantly related to higher likelihood judgments.
text.formatted: As displayed in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">S9</ref> (also see Table <ref type="table">S9</ref> for test statistics), for utopia, mentioning Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Prabowo Subianto, Narendra Modi, or Javier Milei was statistically significantly related to higher likelihood judgments.

text.text: Mentioning Vladimir Putin was statistically significantly related to lower likelihood judgments.

In terms of dystopia, findings were much more uniform, with mentioning eight leaders being associated with higher likelihood judgments and one leader (i.e., Adolf Hitler) with lower likelihood judgments.

Exploratory analyses also showed that mentioning the leaders was with a few exceptions associated with higher leader attribution, whereas no consistent pattern was observed for self-attribution (see Figure S10).
text.formatted: Exploratory analyses also showed that mentioning the leaders was with a few exceptions associated with higher leader attribution, whereas no consistent pattern was observed for self-attribution (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">S10</ref>).

text.text: Exploratory tests showed that these effects interacted with participants' own political orientation (see Table S8).
text.formatted: Exploratory tests showed that these effects interacted with participants' own political orientation (see Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>).

text.text: Political orientation moderated the mention ratio for 6 of the 14 most mentioned leaders.
However, simple slopes only indicated a systematic pattern for two leaders (see Figure S8).
text.formatted: However, simple slopes only indicated a systematic pattern for two leaders (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">S8</ref>).

text.text: The tendency to name Donald Trump in the dystopian condition decreased as participants became more politically conservative (but no inverse effect was observed for utopia).
Moreover, Xi Jinping was named increasingly in the dystopia and decreasingly in the utopia condition as participants became more conservative.

Every unique leader name with a non-negative cluster ID was classified on three ideological dimensions by GPT-4o-mini, strictly following the rubric below: If a leader fits multiple categories, choose the most prominent.
If info is insufficient, output "NA".

The model returned valid JSON containing a one-to-five social political score (from 1 very liberal to 5 very conservative), a one-to-five economic political orientation score (from 1 very liberal to 5 very conservative), and an eight-category taxonomic class (79), or "NA" if confidence fell below fifty percent.
The automatic political orientation scoring was validated by three human experts who rated sixty-five randomly sampled leaders on the same five-point social and economic scales.
Their mutual reliability was α = 0.88 for social and 0.74 for economic.
The correlation between the averaged human ratings and GPT scores reached .88 on the social dimension and .70 on the economic dimension, both statistically significant at p < .001.
text.formatted: The correlation between the averaged human ratings and GPT scores reached .88 on the social dimension and .70 on the economic dimension, both statistically significant at p < .001.

text.text: For the categorical taxonomy, two separate coders classified seventy leaders.
Using Fleiss PABAK the within-human agreement ranged from .54 to .91 across the eight classes, and the machine-human agreement ranged from .77 to 1.00.
With the classified data, we conducted three tests comparing the political orientation of the leaders mentioned in the two conditions.
We first tested for the taxonomy by Gunther and Diamond (79).

text.text: As displayed in Figure S11, the rank of the first three categories was the same in both conditions, with nationalist mass-based leaders mentioned most often, followed by electoralist and socialist mass-based leaders.

text.text: Direct comparisons were then conducted between the two conditions using the same statistical approach as for leader names.
Extreme right, elite-based, and nationalist mass-based leaders were more likely to be mentioned in the dystopian condition, see Table S10.
text.formatted: Extreme right, elite-based, and nationalist mass-based leaders were more likely to be mentioned in the dystopian condition, see Table <ref type="table">S10</ref>.

text.text: Electoralist, religious mass-based and leftlibertarian leaders were more likely to be mentioned in the utopia condition.
No significant difference was observed for socialist mass-based leaders.
Exploratory tests showed that the effect of condition interacted with participants' political orientation (see Table S11, Figure S12).
text.formatted: Exploratory tests showed that the effect of condition interacted with participants' political orientation (see Table <ref type="table">S11</ref>, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_16">S12</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, the more conservative participants were, they less likely they were to mention electoralist and social mass-based leaders in the utopia condition and somewhat more likely to mention them in the dystopia condition.

By contrast, the more conservative participants were, the more likely they were to mention extreme-right and nationalist mass-based leaders in the utopia condition and the less likely they were to mention nationalist mass-based leaders in the dystopia condition.

Again based on cross-national analyses presented in the Shiny App (https://dystopia-utopia.shinyapps.io/country/), under the utopia condition, nationalist massbased leaders were the clear front-runners, topping the list in 29 countries and placing second in nine.

text.text: The secondary category in the utopia condition was electoralist / mediadriven leaders, which held the first spot in eight cells and came in second in 23.
In the dystopia condition, nationalist mass-based again led overwhelmingly, ranking first in 37 cells and second in three (i.e., they were in the top two dystopia mentions for every country).
The next most cited category was socialist mass-based, which was first in two countries and second in eight.
Finally, we tested whether the continuous ideological leaning of the leaders that respondents named differed between the utopia and dystopia conditions.

For each respondent, we first separately averaged separate social and economic ideology scores of all leaders they mentioned in the case they mentioned several leaders (higher scores for both measures = more conservative).
We then fit two separate linear mixed-effects models with condition as a predictor and with random intercepts and effects for country.

As pre-registered, in an exploratory analysis, we tested the effects of scenario condition and leader condition on leader attribution using a 2 x 2 ANOVA.

There was a significant main effect of scenario condition on leader attribution, F(1, 1989) = 15.88, p < .001, ηp² = .01, bootstrap 95% CI [.00, .02], such that participants in the dystopia condition (M = 6.48, SD = 3.11) perceived higher leader attribution than those in the utopia condition (M = 5.93, SD = 3.26), model-estimated marginal mean difference = .43, 95% CI [.22, .64], t(1989) = 3.99, p < .001, d = .18, 95% CI [.09, .27].

To test whether the main effect differed across countries, as pre-registered, we conducted a 2 (Condition: Utopia/Dystopia) x 4 (Country: India/Mexico/South Africa/USA) ANOVA for likelihood judgment.

The results indicated a significant main effect of Country (F(3, 759) = 15.10, p < .001, bootstrap p < .001, η²p = .06, bootstrap 95%CI [.03, .10]) and Condition (F(1, 759) = 172.46, p <. 001, bootstrap p < .001, η²p = .19, bootstrap 95%CI [.14, .24]).
text.formatted: The results indicated a significant main effect of Country (F(3, 759) = 15.10, p < .001, bootstrap p < .001, η²p = .06, bootstrap 95%CI [.03, .10]) and Condition (F(1, 759) = 172.46, p <. 001, bootstrap p < .001, η²p = .19, bootstrap 95%CI [.14, .24]).

text.text: No significant interaction effect between Country and Condition was found, F(3, 759) = 1.53, p = .205, bootstrap p = .176, η²p = .01, bootstrap 95%CI [.00, .02].

Post hoc testing using Tukey's HSD showed that across all countries, participants in the dystopia condition scored 2.59 points higher on the likelihood judgment scale than participants in the utopia condition, 95%CI [2.20, 2.98], pTukey < .001.
text.formatted: Post hoc testing using Tukey's HSD showed that across all countries, participants in the dystopia condition scored 2.59 points higher on the likelihood judgment scale than participants in the utopia condition, 95%CI [2.20, 2.98], pTukey < .001.

text.text: Furthermore, there was a significant difference in likelihood judgment between all countries (all ps < .01), except for South Africa and Mexico (p = .999).
text.formatted: Furthermore, there was a significant difference in likelihood judgment between all countries (all ps < .01), except for South Africa and Mexico (p = .999).

text.text: The biggest mean difference occurred between the USA and India with American participants scoring on average 1.89 points lower on the likelihood judgment scale than participants from India, 95%CI [-2.61, -1.17], pTukey < .001.
text.formatted: The biggest mean difference occurred between the USA and India with American participants scoring on average 1.89 points lower on the likelihood judgment scale than participants from India, 95%CI [-2.61, -1.17], pTukey < .001.

text.text: We ran an exploratory multi-group parallel mediation using structural equation modeling to determine whether the effect of condition on likelihood was mediated via our three attribution judgments.
Participants were grouped by country (i.e., India, Mexico, South Africa, USA).
We used the maximum likelihood estimator and applied bootstrapping with 5,000 re-samples.
We first ran an unconstrained model, allowing all parameters to be estimated freely across countries.
Next, we constrained each path separately to test differences in model fit using Wald tests.

When constraining path b3 (i.e., the path from luck to likelihood), a Wald test showed model fit was significantly worse compared to the baseline model (p = .049), indicating differences between countries for this path.
Constraining any of the other paths did not significantly worsen model fit (all ps > .05), suggesting no significant difference between the countries for these paths.
text.formatted: Constraining any of the other paths did not significantly worsen model fit (all ps > .05), suggesting no significant difference between the countries for these paths.

text.text: Therefore, in the final, partially constrained model, we allowed path b3 (i.e., luck to likelihood) to vary freely across countries, but constrained all other paths.

This partially constrained model was not inferior to the fully unconstrained model (Δχ2(18)= 19.05, p = .389) and showed very good fit (χ2(18)=19.05, p = .389, RMSEA = .017, CFI = .998, TLI = .995, SRMR = .035).
Neither self attribution nor luck mediated the relationship between condition and likelihood, see Figure S3.
text.formatted: Neither self attribution nor luck mediated the relationship between condition and likelihood, see Figure <ref type="figure">S3</ref>.

text.text: The total indirect effect of condition on likelihood was significant in the USA (β = .04, b = .20, 95% CI [.01, .39], SE = .10, z = 2.03, p = .042), but not in India, Mexico, or South Africa (all ps > .05).
text.formatted: The total indirect effect of condition on likelihood was significant in the USA (β = .04, b = .20, 95% CI [.01, .39], SE = .10, z = 2.03, p = .042), but not in India, Mexico, or South Africa (all ps > .05).

text.text: The total effect of the condition on likelihood judgment was positive and significant for all countries (all ps < .001, βs >. 46).

text.text: To test whether particular leaders were more (or less) likely to be named when participants had thought of a dystopia versus a utopia, we first isolated the 14 names that formed the union of each condition's ten most-frequent answers.

For every one of these leaders, we created a respondent-level binary flag (1 = leader mentioned at least once,0 = not mentioned/no leader mentioned) and fitted a separate mixed-effects logistic regression with condition (reference = utopia) as the sole fixed effect and a random intercept for country (adding random slopes led to convergence issues).

Topic Analysis.
A BERTopic analysis (64) was conducted to better understand what people envisioned in the utopia versus dystopia condition.
On average, participants wrote M = 17.85 words, SD = 21.37, in the utopia and M = 15.24 words, SD = 11.78 in the dystopia condition.
We ran one topic model per conditions.

Used for Classification of Leaders' Political Orientations: =================================================================== SOCIAL and ECONOMIC ideological dimensions =================================================================== Social dimension -Objective Rate each leader from 1 (Very liberal) to 5 (Very conservative).

Consider social equality vs. hierarchy, individual liberty vs. social order, traditional vs. progressive values, state intervention vs. individual responsibility, and civil-liberties/human-rights records. -1 Very liberal -Revolutionary transformation of social hierarchies; dismantle capitalism, patriarchy, racism, imperialism; egalitarian society. -2 Liberal -Progressive reforms within existing institutions; incremental change; social justice, equality, inclusivity, civil rights, healthcare access, environmental justice. -3 Neutral -Pragmatic compromise; gradual evidence-based change; stability and empathy; midpoint between 2 and 4. -4 Conservative -Individual freedom, limited state intervention; traditional values balanced with rights; family values, local empowerment. -5 Very conservative -Strict traditional norms; nationalist / xenophobic rhetoric; antiimmigration; oppose LGBTQ+ rights; rigid gender roles.
*Dictators*: judge by policies, not rhetoric.
Economic dimension -Objective Rate each leader from 1 (Very liberal) to 5 (Very conservative).

Consider state role, market regulation, redistribution, taxation, public vs. private ownership, trade, labour rights, welfare, etc. -1 Very liberal -Communism/Marxism/anarchism; anti-capitalist; radical overhaul. -2 Liberal -Redistribution, progressive taxes, expansive welfare, strong regulation. -3 Neutral -Balanced pragmatists; combine markets with regulation; targeted social programmes; moderated free trade. -4 Conservative -Laissez-faire leaning; market freedom, privatisation; limited welfare and regulation. -5 Very conservative -Near-total laissez-faire: deregulation, minimal taxes, widespread privatisation, deep cuts to public spending.
*Dictators*: judge by actions, not statements.
